{{No footnotes|date=June 2022}}
In [[mathematics]], particularly [[topology]], a '''cosmic space''' is any [[topological space]] that is a [[continuous function|continuous]] [[Image (mathematics)|image]] of some [[Separable space|separable]] [[metric space]]. Equivalently (for [[regular space|regular]] [[T1 space|''T''<sub>1</sub> spaces]] but not in general), a space is cosmic if and only if it has a [[countable]] network; namely a [[countable set|countable]] collection of [[subset]]s of the space such that any [[open set]] is the [[Union (set theory)|union]] of a subcollection of these sets.

Cosmic spaces have several interesting properties. There are a number of unsolved problems about them.

==Examples and properties==

* Any open subset of a cosmic space is cosmic since open subsets of separable spaces are separable.
* Separable metric spaces are trivially cosmic.

==Unsolved problems==

It is unknown as to whether ''X'' is cosmic if:

a) ''X''<sup>2</sup> contains no uncountable [[discrete space]];

b) the countable product of ''X'' with itself is hereditarily separable and hereditarily [[Lindelöf space|Lindelöf]].
